articles.title: UK says new deal will ‘rebuild bridges’ with EU: What’s in it?
articles.summary: Agreements aim to simplify trade checks, link emissions systems and launch a youth mobility programme.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom and the European Union have struck a deal aimed at mending fences and repairing the economic fallout caused by Brexit, a decade after UK voters opted to leave the bloc.

At a joint news conference following the EU-UK summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal would “rebuild the bridges that were broken all those years ago”. He hailed the agreements as “a good deal for Britain”.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said there was an “intensive” debate on how much the world has changed since Brexit, during the meeting.

The COVID pandemic “was not even over when Russia started the war in Ukraine”, she said. “We have stuck together from day one on.

“We can always work on an incremental improvement of our relationship, but as I said, we are totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture.”

The agreements cover three areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies.

But disagreements remain, particularly over university tuition fees.

Burnham also faces political resistance at home over how far strengthening ties with the EU should go.

Three main agreements were on the table at the summit between Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

The first would remove checks and reduce paperwork on food and agricultural products traded between Britain and the EU, making exports easier and potentially lowering costs for businesses and consumers. That could be good news for businesspeople like Tim Jones , an English cheesemaker whom Al Jazeera recently interviewed.

The second would link the two sides’ emissions-trading systems, which would give an exemption to goods from Britain and the EU, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.

The third establishes a youth mobility programme allowing up to 100,000 people under 30 from each side to live in the other’s territory for up to three years for work, study or travel.

Burnham said the agreements could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s gross domestic product (GDP), raising his previous estimate of 0.4 percent.

The prime minister described the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.

Despite the breakthrough, hurdles remain, among them university tuition fees. Brussels wants EU students attending British universities to pay the same domestic rates as British students rather than the substantially higher international fees currently charged.

London has resisted the proposal, which could have significant financial implications for universities.

“We have not yet reached an agreement on tuition fees, and we have given ourselves six months to reach that agreement,” an EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters.

Another unresolved issue concerns Britain’s demand for access to the EU’s “made in Europe” rules, notably for cars.

“Made in Europe” is part of the EU’s planned Industrial Accelerator Act and is aimed primarily at forcing Chinese automakers to produce cars within the bloc using local suppliers in order to qualify for key subsidies and bid for government procurement contracts.

The EU has indicated it is willing to grant this but on the condition that London aligns with its policies, which restrict imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

Burnham has indicated that his government will examine longer-term options, ranging from maintaining existing arrangements to joining the EU customs union or eventually rejoining the bloc.

“After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship,” he said.

But rejoining would require support from British voters and unanimous approval from EU member states, making any immediate return unlikely.

Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from Brussels, said there was “no actual signing” expected on Friday. “There’s no document being inked,” she said.

A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera, “As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place … and talks will continue on some areas.”

Where do other UK political parties stand?

The negotiations have divided the UK’s political landscape.

Within Burnham’s Labour Party, some politicians support rebuilding European ties but fear reopening the divisive Brexit debate.

“I’m happy with closer ties, but he does need to tread carefully,” one Labour MP told the AFP news agency.

The opposition Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK have predictably criticised the government’s direction. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Farage, who led the Brexit campaign, told the BBC.

He warned that the discussion would soon become one about whether Britain should rejoin the EU.

A YouGov poll published on Wednesday suggested 54 percent of UK citizens think “it would be acceptable to have a rejoin referendum in the next five years” but are divided over whether it is a top priority.

European officials, meanwhile, have remained cautious about Britain’s longer-term intentions.

Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador in London, said there was “a lack of clarity” about what Brexit meant. If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants”.

images.caption: From left, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa arrive for the EU-UK Summit in Brussels on November 20, 2026 [Yves Herman, Pool Photo via AP Photo]

articles.title: Hot potato: Can Japan resist Trump pressure to import food staple?
articles.summary: Japan imports 60 percent of its food, but it fiercely draws the line at potatoes.
articles.body:
For the first time in 76 years, the country may be forced to lift a ban on United States potato imports under intense pressure from President Donald Trump.

The proposal, which has not been confirmed yet, is already prompting strong opposition from Japanese potato farmers who said the move could expose their crops to harmful foreign pests and diseases from imported batches. They also said cheap imports would impact their own sales.

The US first requested that Japan lift its import ban in 2020 during Trump’s first term. Now Washington has turned up the heat. In March, lawmakers urged Trump to discuss the matter during a planned meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Tokyo has begun seriously considering the matter – possibly to use as a bargaining chip during Trump’s trade and tariff wars, observers said.

The issue was discussed again when Japanese officials visited Washington, DC, in September. Now, Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries is moving forward by first identifying potential problems, including diseases and pests, and then seeking measures from the US to avoid them, Japanese media reported.

Is Japan ready to toe Trump’s line on potatoes despite sure backlash at home? Here’s what we know:

Japan imports 60 percent of its food, but raw potatoes and rice are where it has always drawn the line.

Potatoes hold historical and cultural significance and form the base of some of the country’s most popular dishes, including nikujaga, a meal of simmered meat and potatoes, and the baked, butter-topped dish known as jaga bata.

In post-World War II Japan, more readily available potatoes and sweet potatoes helped prevent a famine as alternative staples, such as rice, were strictly rationed.

To keep its potato fields free from infestation by foreign pests, Japan placed a ban on potato imports in 1950.

Since 2006, only US potatoes used exclusively to produce crisps are allowed in – and only under strict conditions. The potatoes must be imported in sealed containers and must be transferred to factories where they are first cooked at high heat to kill any harmful diseases or pests.

Japan’s Agriculture Ministry has noted at least 21 pests and diseases that could infect the country’s potatoes if the ban is lifted. Officials said they plan to discuss possible measures to reduce the risks.

There is a particular fear of cyst nematodes – tiny worm-like insects that damage potato roots and remain in the soil for many years. In 2015, authorities discovered the insects in parts of the northern island of Hokkaido. Affected areas are still under restrictions.

“Once pests get in, you can’t grow potatoes for more than a decade,” Hokkaido farmer Naohiro Makino told the Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun in September.

Farmers on the island produce about 80 percent of Japan’s potatoes. If the infestation of 2015 were to recur on a wider scale, farmers fear Japan’s potato production could be threatened.

“For the sake of the farmland our ancestors protected, I am firmly opposed,” Makino added.

A Japanese investigation into possible disease or pest outcomes is a sign that authorities are considering lifting the ban.

But there is pushback from farmers and agricultural cooperatives from Hokkaido and elsewhere. They’ve submitted petitions to the Agriculture Ministry stating their opposition and have conducted rallies.

One online briefing by the ministry drew hundreds of farmers. “Why do we need to import potatoes when Japan is already self-sufficient?” one participant asked.

On Monday, Hokkaido Governor Suzuki Naomichi urged authorities to take a firm stance and defend Japan’s interests during the potato talks.

The governor was speaking to Agriculture Minister Takebe Arata, who said talks with the US would only proceed after Japan had thoroughly discussed scientific evidence.

Officials have repeatedly stated that Japan is obliged to consider the US requests under its international agreements. They’ve floated possible protection measures like inspections, but farmers have remained sceptical.

“I hope the government will handle the talks in line with our request and his remarks,” Naomichi said, referring to the minister’s promises.

images.caption: Demonstrators protest against allowing US potato imports into Japan on October 13, 2026, outside the Agriculture Ministry in Tokyo, Japan [Josia Kasahara/NurPhoto via Getty Images]
A field under solar panels at a farm growing sweet potatoes in the city of Chiba, Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo, in November 2023 [File: Philip Fong/AFP]

articles.title: Saudi coalition and Houthis exchange threats to bomb key ports
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis have warned airlines of military activity in Saudi airspace in the coming hours.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-led coalition have exchanged threats to bomb key ports in the latest round of escalation between the warring parties.

⁠On Friday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi Arabia’s Red ⁠⁠Sea ports if Saudi-led coalition forces follow through on threats to strike the Houthi-held Yemeni ⁠⁠port city of Hodeidah. The Iran-backed armed group also warned airlines to stay out of Saudi airspace because it was planning ⁠new strikes within hours.

The threats come a day after the Houthis struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh , raising fears of further escalation in a conflict that has caused a humanitarian crisis in Yemen and severe disruption in ⁠⁠Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the wider US-led war against Iran.

On Friday, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government urged civilians ⁠⁠to evacuate areas of Hodeidah port for their safety, without providing further details.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree then responded on X, saying that Jeddah port and all Saudi ports on the Red Sea coast would become “targets” if the coalition carried out its threat to strike Hodeidah port.

“We warn all employees, workers, and those in the vicinity of [Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea] ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away. We also urge all shipping companies to immediately evacuate their ships from these ports,” he said.

Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace “because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours”, Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia.

Shortly afterwards, the Saudi-led coalition said on X that it had begun a “targeted operation” against Houthi assets it claimed are being used to target civilians in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“We targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles,” spokesman Turki al-Malki wrote, adding that operations were “ongoing” in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz governorates.

In Sanaa, which is the Houthi-held Yemeni capital, the coalition said it targeted the Houthis’ ballistic missile and drone capabilities.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said there are “warnings from both sides and both sides seem to be delivering on their promise to step up their aerial assault”.

He said a number of Saudi coalition air strikes and drones targeted the city on Friday morning. The targets included what the coalition claimed were military sites and workshops used to produce ballistic missiles and drones.

Meanwhile, the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – launched a series of their own attacks and issued warnings that they would attack other sites, he said.

“Both sides seem to be stepping up their attacks. These are the heaviest air strikes that we have witnessed since the conflict began. And both sides seem to carry a very serious tone in delivering on their promise to target [sites including] energy infrastructure and airports,” Mawry added.

Fighting is raging in other parts of Yemen , with the Houthis advancing on the government’s de facto capital of Aden in recent weeks. Government forces are now preparing for the defence of the coastal city – their last real stronghold.

The Houthis also continue to besiege the government-held city of Taiz, north of Aden. That city has now been cut off from Aden, and residents have complained of shortages of water and fuel.

images.caption: The Saudi-led coalition has carried out air strikes against the Houthis to try to halt their advance on the government-held Yemeni cities of Taiz and Aden [Yahya Arhab/EPA]

articles.title: Putin launches Ukraine barrage hours after Trump meeting amid alleged Russian missile breach of NATO airspace
articles.summary: Hours after Vladimir Putin joined Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing at least eight.
articles.body: Just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin stood alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit in China, Moscow unleashed one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, killing at least eight people, striking three major bridges in Kyiv and sending suspected Russian missiles and a drone into NATO-member Poland. The massive overnight assault Friday came as the Trump administration announced progress toward expanding peace negotiations with Russia, exposing the stark contrast between the diplomatic optimism emerging from Thursday's meetings and the escalating war on the ground. A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that Putin is preparing an intensified winter military campaign and believes that a combination of sustained battlefield pressure and U.S.-led diplomatic negotiations could eventually force Ukraine to surrender additional territory. TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE The source described the photograph of Putin standing alongside Trump and Xi as a long-sought diplomatic achievement for the Russian leader, even as Moscow prepares to increase pressure on Kyiv. According to the source, Russia's calculation is that Ukraine could be compelled to accept territorial concessions by spring, particularly in the country's east. "They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source told Fox News Digital, describing what the source assessed to be Moscow's strategy. The source also warned that Russian military pressure is increasing despite Ukraine's recent successful strikes against critical Russian infrastructure. "It's going to be a very difficult winter for Ukrainians," the source said. Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that the timing of Russia's latest assault should leave little doubt about Putin's intentions, arguing that the Russian leader has repeatedly responded to President Donald Trump's diplomatic overtures with renewed attacks on Ukraine. "Putin never has been a partner for peace in Ukraine," he said. "And Putin will never be a partner for peace in the future for Ukraine." Breedlove said that Putin's objective is to subjugate Ukraine, install a leadership loyal to Moscow and exploit the country's resources. RUSSIA PLOTTING 'MASSIVE STRIKE' DURING MIDTERMS, ZELENSKYY WARNS, URGES US TO STOP PUTIN Russia launches massive attack on Ukrainian cities Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, targeting the country's energy, transportation and logistical infrastructure. The barrage killed six people in Kyiv and two in the western city of Lviv, while more than two dozen others were wounded, according to a Reuters' Nov. 20 report. Three major bridges spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges — were struck, disrupting transportation between the eastern and western sections of the capital. Russian attacks also damaged railway infrastructure and energy facilities, triggering emergency power outages as temperatures drop ahead of winter. In Lviv, two people were killed in a strike on the Sknyliv railway station, while additional injuries were reported following attacks on residential buildings and a hospital in other Ukrainian regions. UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL' Zelenskyy accused Moscow of using the attacks to compensate for what he described as military and diplomatic setbacks. "This was one of the largest attacks," Zelenskyy said in a statement published on Telegram Friday. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out a massive operation, saying it targeted facilities connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex, including missile and drone production sites and transportation infrastructure. The competing claims about the targets and the extent of the damage could not be independently verified. The strikes followed Putin's warning Thursday that Russia would retaliate against Ukraine for repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula. Ukrainian forces launched three attacks on the strategic crossing in four days, damaging its road section and disrupting rail traffic. The bridge, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, serves as both a transportation route and a powerful symbol of Moscow's control over Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014. UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA Russian missiles enter NATO-member Poland The overnight assault also raised concerns beyond Ukraine's borders after Polish officials reported three separate incursions into the country's airspace. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one of the objects was identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while another was believed to be a missile and the third likely a jet-powered drone. Authorities were investigating debris near Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in southeastern Poland. "There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Kosiniak-Kamysz said, according to Reuters. Poland said it would seek additional NATO assistance to secure the alliance's eastern flank. Breedlove warned that the reported incursions into Polish airspace were part of a broader pattern of Russia testing NATO's resolve. "Mr. Putin will push further and further when there is no cost to him, when NATO doesn't respond, when the United States doesn't respond, in his mind, there is no reason to stop. He will continue," Breedlove told Fox News Digital. UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA Putin's strategy as peace talks advance The attacks came less than a day after the Trump administration announced what it described as progress toward a broader diplomatic framework involving Russia, Ukraine and European governments. During talks in Berlin Thursday, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow had agreed to engage in an expanded negotiating format that would include European representatives. "Russia has agreed to engage in the multilateral format with the Europeans," Kushner said, according to Fox News Digital's Nov. 19 report. Zelenskyy urged Washington to organize the next round of discussions quickly, insisting that European governments must play a full role in negotiations affecting the continent's security. But Moscow's position remained less clear Friday, with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov saying an invitation for European officials to visit Moscow did not mean they had been accepted into the existing U.S.-brokered negotiating format, according to The Associated Press. The European intelligence source suggested Russia believes the diplomatic process itself could strengthen its negotiating position by allowing Moscow to broaden discussions beyond Ukrainian territory to the future security arrangements of Europe. According to the source, Moscow is seeking to gain time, maintain military pressure and increasingly focus negotiations on wider European security questions. The source also described Russian efforts to maintain troop numbers without announcing another large-scale nationwide mobilization. "They have been able to avoid open mobilization, but they have hidden mobilization," the source said. According to the source, Russian recruitment efforts include targeting people facing financial difficulties, debt or other social vulnerabilities, alongside continued recruitment from prisons. RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA The source argued that Moscow is prioritizing manpower over the quality and training of new recruits. "More quantity, less quality," the source said, warning that inadequately prepared recruits face a greater risk of being killed on the battlefield. Those recruitment claims have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital. The source's broader assessment was that Russia believes it can sustain military operations long enough to increase pressure on Ukraine's leadership to accept territorial concessions. For Kyiv, the latest barrage demonstrated the immediate challenge facing U.S.-led peace efforts: negotiations are advancing while Moscow continues large-scale military operations and Ukraine strikes strategic targets deep inside Russian-held territory. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The events also highlighted the growing risks for NATO as the consequences of Russia's war extend beyond Ukraine's borders. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations
articles.summary: The incidents came as European troops were taking part in a Ukraine post-war military exercise.
articles.body:
Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west.

Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the three objects were probably two missiles and a drone.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “ Coalition of the Willing “, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.

The potential crash site near Nowy Lipowiec is about 76km (47 miles) from where European troops were taking part in military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine, aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.

“These exercises, combined with the presence of defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states – along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies – suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

The defence minister said Poland would ask NATO for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that NATO stood in solidarity with Poland.

Tusk said Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday. The Polish prime minister added that there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian.

“It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation,” he said. “Today, it is clearer than ever before that ⁠Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe.”

British ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Russia’s violation of Polish airspace, calling it “utterly ⁠unacceptable”.

“Europe will not be ⁠deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said at an EU-UK summit news conference in ‌Brussels. “We will not allow [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to divide our continent, and ‌we recognise that the front line in Ukraine is the front line for freedom and democracy everywhere.”

Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance and stoking fears that the conflict ⁠could spread.

The incident in Poland came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed eight people, injured dozens more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure.

articles.title: Cheese aged in military fortress founded by Napoleon just named best in the world
articles.summary: Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months, a raw cow's milk cheese aged for two years in a French fortress, won the 2026 World Cheese Awards in Córdoba, Spain.
articles.body: A cheese made from raw cow’s milk and aged for two years in a historic military fortress in France just took home the top prize in the 2026 World Cheese Awards, a global competition that judged more than 5,000 cheeses from over 40 countries. Held in Córdoba, Spain, on Nov. 12, the annual showcase aims to highlight local cheesemaking and food and drink culture, according to the Guild of Fine Food, which organizes the World Cheese Awards. This year, the judges’ overall winning pick was Fromageries Arnaud's Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months, which gets its name from the former military fortress Fort des Rousses in eastern France, near the Swiss border. AMERICA'S BEST PIZZERIAS CROWNED IN NEW RANKINGS AS PIZZA EXPERT GIVES SLICE OF SKEPTICISM Founded in the early 1800s by Napoleon Bonaparte, who viewed the location as "a strategic military position," according to the historic fort’s website, Fort des Rousses served as a military base and training camp before eventually being turned into aging cellars in 1998. With 50,000 square meters of vaulted stone cellars, the fortress is one of France’s largest cheese caves, housing nearly 140,000 wheels of Comté, the fort’s website says. Comté is a cooked and pressed cheese made from unpasteurized cow’s milk traditionally made in the Jura Massif mountain region of France, according to Comté USA. A young Comté typically smells of butter, dried apricots and caramel. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Meanwhile, a Comté that’s aged for a long time will be more fruity, spicy and nutty, the organization’s website states. The Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months was aged by cheese maturer, or affineur, JuraFlore, which has been aging cheeses since 1907. Their Charles Arnaud cellar in Fort des Rousses, which produced this year’s world champion, is dedicated solely to Comté cheeses, according to the website. articles.title: In 2019, a North Carolina property owner says flooding from a 361-home development battered her land and fences; seven years later, an appeals court has rejected the city's immunity defence
articles.summary: A North Carolina property owner who accused a city of allowing stormwater from a large residential development to repeatedly flood her land has won an
articles.body: A North Carolina property owner who accused a city of allowing stormwater from a large residential development to repeatedly flood her land has won an important procedural victory after years of litigation. The dispute began in 2019, when a flash flood allegedly sent several feet of muddy water, construction debris and other material onto her property, damaging fences and an underground stormwater pipe.In a November 18, 2026, decision available on Justia, the North Carolina Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's refusal to dismiss the claims against the City of Concord on governmental immunity grounds. The judges ruled that the city's stormwater management activities were proprietary functions rather than governmental functions, meaning the city could not use governmental immunity to avoid the negligence, trespass and private nuisance claims at this stage. The decision allows the lawsuit to proceed but does not establish that the city was responsible for the alleged damage.Flash floods followed construction of 361-home developmentThe case, Moss v. City of Concord, involved Jaylene Moss and RWJ Consulting Inc., whose property was located in Concord, North Carolina. The City of Concord owned an easement for underground pipes running through their land. In 2014, the city approved plans for a residential development south of the property that would eventually consist of 361 large, single-family homes. It approved the second and third phases of the development in 2016.According to the plaintiffs' complaint, a rainstorm in 2019 caused a flash flood during construction, sending several feet of brown water from the development site onto their property. The flooding allegedly carried wood debris and discarded fast-food cups from the construction area, washed away sections of the northern fence and destroyed the southern fence.The property owners also alleged that the force of the water, combined with tree debris from the construction site, caused an underground stormwater pipe beneath their front yard to buckle and break. The damage reportedly created a hole measuring approximately two feet by two feet. The problem did not end with the first incident. The plaintiffs alleged that several additional flash floods occurred between 2020 and 2024, continuing to affect their property.Property owners accused city of inadequate stormwater managementIn 2022, Moss and RWJ Consulting filed a lawsuit against the City of Concord and several other parties involved in the development. These included Tac Niblock LLC, Landworks Design Group PA, The Ardent Companies LLC, CMG Builders Inc. and Hunton Forest Homeowner's Association Inc. The complaint included claims of negligence, trespass and private nuisance. The plaintiffs alleged that the city had approved the development's stormwater design without ensuring that the system could adequately manage the volume and flow of water generated by construction.They also accused the city of failing to monitor the stormwater system, enforce maintenance requirements and prevent recurring overflows onto their land. In addition, they brought an inverse condemnation claim, arguing that the city's actions had effectively resulted in a taking of their property. The city sought dismissal, arguing that governmental immunity protected it from the claims. However, on June 4, 2025, the Cabarrus County Superior Court denied the city's motion, finding that the complaint contained claims on which relief could be granted. The city then appealed that decision.Appeals court distinguishes governmental and proprietary functionsThe central question before the appeals court was whether the city's involvement in stormwater management qualified as a governmental function protected by immunity. Under North Carolina law, municipalities generally enjoy governmental immunity when performing governmental functions. However, that protection does not automatically extend to proprietary activities, which are commercial or undertaken primarily for the private advantage of a community.The court noted that North Carolina law classifies stormwater management as a public enterprise under N.C. General Statutes Section 160A-311(10). It also relied on a 2024 decision, Devonwood-Loch Lomond Lake Association Inc. v. City of Fayetteville, in which the court had ruled that stormwater management was a proprietary municipal function and that related negligence, trespass and nuisance claims were not barred by governmental immunity.Applying the same reasoning, the judges concluded that the allegations against Concord concerned its proprietary stormwater management activities. Therefore, the city could not rely on governmental immunity to obtain dismissal of those claims.Lawsuit can proceed, but liability remains undecidedThe North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's June 2025 order denying the city's motion to dismiss on governmental immunity grounds. However, the judges declined to consider the city's separate challenge to the inverse condemnation claim because that issue was not properly before them in the interlocutory appeal. They also denied the city's request for discretionary review of that issue.The ruling does not determine whether the city negligently handled stormwater management or whether it must compensate the property owners. Those questions remain for further proceedings. The decision means that the plaintiffs can continue pursuing their negligence, trespass and nuisance claims without the city using governmental immunity as a defence at this stage.You use AI every day. articles.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
articles.summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
articles.body:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

articles.title: Indian man gets 19-plus years in assassination plot of Sikh leader
articles.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
articles.body:
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed by the Indian government.

The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

articles.title: UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
articles.summary: Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK.
articles.body:
A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom.

Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board.

Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel.

“They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added.

Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat ⁠⁠carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred ⁠⁠onto another vessel and taken ashore.

The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident.

Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the ⁠⁠boat … take them back, no more ⁠⁠of these”.

Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of ‌‌the incident was played.

Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate ‌‌attempt ‌‌to disrupt rescue efforts.

The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats.

A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”.

The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping.

Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March.

UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

articles.title: Vietnam narrows death penalty to four crimes, drops drug trafficking from list
articles.summary: Vietnam has narrowed the use of capital punishment to just four crimes under a revised penal code passed by the National Assembly on Friday.
articles.body: Vietnam has narrowed the use of capital punishment to just four crimes under a revised penal code passed by the National Assembly on Friday.The death sentence will now be reserved for treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production. Drug trafficking, crimes against humanity, war crimes, rebellion and the rape of a juvenile have been removed from the list of offences punishable by death, with life imprisonment becoming the maximum sentence for these crimes.The move marks another step in Vietnam's gradual reduction of capital offences. The country's 1985 penal code had listed 44 crimes that could attract the death penalty.The decision comes despite reservations among some lawmakers about removing capital punishment for drug trafficking, a serious offence in the Southeast Asian country.Minister of public security Luong Tam Quang defended the change, saying evidence showed that some people involved in drug trafficking had been “lured, cheated or forced” into committing the offences.“They can still be rehabilitated, educated and given the chance to make amends for their actions,” he said, adding that imposing the death penalty was therefore unnecessary.Vietnam uses lethal injection for executions after abandoning firing squads in 2013. However, the government has never publicly disclosed the number of people it has executed.Amnesty International estimated that more than 1,200 people were on death row in Vietnam at the end of 2023. articles.title: Government blocks export of landmark Llannerch Park painting
articles.summary: The "remarkable" landscape painting of Llannerch Park in Denbighshire was completed in 1662.
articles.body:
A painting believed to be the earliest known British country estate landscape has been barred from export to give a gallery or institution the chance to acquire it, the UK government has said.

The bird's-eye view landscape artwork of Llannerch Park, in Denbighshire, north Wales, was completed in 1662 and depicts the house and Italian-style gardens.

It has been described as an "extraordinary window into the development of gardens" and a heritage expert said it was "the only surviving evidence of a radical Welsh garden".

The piece has now been placed on a temporary export ban in the hope of keeping it accessible to the UK public.

Llannerch Park garden was created by Royalist landowner Mutton Davies in the 17th Century following a tour of France and Italy - later known as a Grand Tour - and is one of the earliest gardens of its kind in the UK.

The identity of the artist is unknown, but it is believed to have been painted by a British artist due to the presentation of the painting matching the English style.

The oil on canvas painting is 2.3m (7.5ft) wide and 1.6m (5.25ft) high.

It is thought to be the earliest bird's-eye landscape painting of a country estate, said Pippa Shirley, a reviewing committee member of Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (RCEWA).

She said the "remarkable" painting features elaborate fountains, pools, sculptures and Baroque-inspired architecture.

"Nothing remotely like it had been seen in Wales before, and the fact that the garden is now entirely lost makes the painting all the more important," she added.

"It has so much to tell us about early garden history and architecture, patronage and design transmission in Britain that its departure would be a great loss."

The government's export ban stops the piece being taken out of the UK permanently and gives time for museums and galleries to raise the funds needed to acquire the artwork.

Funds could be raised via philanthropic support, or for a private individual to purchase it and donate it to the nation.

Heritage Minister Baroness Twycross said country houses and their gardens were "iconic parts of the British landscape" and that the painting offered an "extraordinary" insight into the development of Welsh and UK landscape artistry.

She added that keeping it in the UK would benefit the public and researchers.

The RCEWA committee made its recommendation on the basis that the painting met the first and third Waverley criteria.

The criteria assesses whether a cultural object proposed for export from the UK is of such national importance that its departure would be a misfortune.

The export licence decision has been deferred until 19 February to allow time for a buyer to come forward and try to purchase the painting.

If there is interest, the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 plus £11,000 VAT.

If an option agreement is signed, a second four-month deferral period will begin.

articles.title: A US postal inspector assigned to stop scams against elderly Americans secretly stole more than $340,000 from intercepted mail, spent the cash on a backyard pool bar and cruises, and has now received 40 months in prison
articles.summary: A former federal law enforcement officer who was responsible for protecting elderly Americans from fraud has been sentenced to 40 months in federal prison
articles.body: A former federal law enforcement officer who was responsible for protecting elderly Americans from fraud has been sentenced to 40 months in federal prison after stealing more than $340,000 in cash from intercepted postal packages. Scott Steven Kelley, 51, of Holden, Massachusetts, worked as a US Postal Inspector investigating fraud schemes targeting older people. However, he was found to have stolen cash that had been recovered from suspected scam victims instead of returning it to them. According to a press release from the US Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts, Kelley used the money to pay for home improvements, including a backyard pool bar, as well as family holidays and cruises.US District Court Judge Margaret R. Guzman handed down the sentence at Worcester federal court on Wednesday, 18 November 2026. Kelley had pleaded guilty in July 2026 to one count of theft of public money, property, or records. Along with the 40-month prison sentence, Judge Guzman ordered him to serve two years of supervised release and pay $343,850 in restitution. "Instead of protecting vulnerable seniors from fraudsters, Scott Kelley victimized them a second time to line his own pockets," US Attorney Leah B. Foley said in a Justice Department statement. "He violated his oath, betrayed the public trust and disgraced the badge he wore."How the mail theft scheme operatedBetween October 2021 and May 2024, Kelley worked as a Team Leader in the Boston Division of the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), according to court documents cited by the Justice Department and reported by MassLive. His job included overseeing investigations into fraud schemes targeting older people across Massachusetts. In many scams targeting elderly people, criminals trick victims into sending large amounts of cash through the postal system. The scammers often pretend to be government officials, lottery representatives or relatives who claim to be facing legal trouble.Postal inspectors are responsible for identifying and intercepting suspicious packages before the money reaches the criminals. The recovered cash is then recorded as evidence and arrangements are made to return it to the victims. However, federal prosecutors said Kelley used his position to steal the money instead. He intercepted at least 17 packages containing cash sent by elderly fraud victims from different parts of the United States. Rather than recording the packages in the official USPIS evidence system, he opened them and kept the cash. The US Attorney's Office confirmed that Kelley stole at least $343,850 from the intercepted packages.Backyard pool bar and holiday spendingFinancial records reviewed by federal investigators showed how Kelley spent the stolen money over nearly three years. According to the Justice Department and WCVB, he deposited the stolen cash into his personal bank accounts and used it to pay credit card bills and other private expenses. Prosecutors said the money also went towards major improvements at his home in Holden. These included the construction of a custom backyard pool bar. Kelley also spent the stolen funds on family holidays, cruises and other personal purchases."Mr. Kelley abandoned his sworn duty to protect the American public and instead chose greed," said Jeffrey B. Veltri, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Boston Division, in the Justice Department's statement. "When a law enforcement officer steals from the very victims he was entrusted to safeguard, it erodes confidence in the justice system."Investigation and accountability inside the postal serviceThe theft came to light after internal checks and federal investigators found problems with records relating to intercepted packages handled under Kelley's supervision. The FBI Boston Division and the US Postal Service Office of Inspector General (USPS OIG) jointly investigated the case, according to the Justice Department. "The vast majority of Postal Inspectors serve with honor and integrity," said Matthew Modafferi, Special Agent in Charge of the USPS Office of Inspector General, in the official statement. "When an employee violates that trust by stealing from vulnerable victims, our agents will work tirelessly with our law enforcement partners to hold them accountable."During the sentencing hearing in Worcester, prosecutors highlighted the additional harm caused to the victims. Many had already lost their savings to fraud schemes before the money was recovered by postal inspectors. They then lost those recovered funds when Kelley stole them instead of returning them. As reported by the Worcester Telegram & Gazette, federal authorities worked to identify the affected people across several states so that recovered money and court-ordered payments could be returned to the rightful owners.Assistant US Attorney Danial E. Bennett of the Worcester Branch Office prosecuted the case. Under federal sentencing rules, Kelley must report to the Bureau of Prisons to begin serving his 40-month prison term. He will also remain legally responsible for repaying the full $343,850 in restitution owed to the victims and the government, in addition to serving two years of supervised release after his prison sentence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kurt Cobain's iconic MTV Unplugged guitar, bought for more than $6 million, was donated to a London music college; the instrument will help students study rock history
articles.summary: Kurt Cobain’s guitar from Nirvana’s celebrated MTV Unplugged performance has found a new home at the Royal College of Music in London, where it will help
articles.body: Kurt Cobain’s guitar from Nirvana’s celebrated MTV Unplugged performance has found a new home at the Royal College of Music in London, where it will help students explore the history of rock music. The instrument, a 1959 Martin D-18E acoustic-electric guitar, was purchased for more than $6 million in 2020 before being donated to the institution by Australian entrepreneur Peter Freedman. The gift brings one of rock music’s most recognisable instruments into an educational setting, while opening opportunities for audiences beyond the college to experience its musical legacy.Kurt Cobain’s MTV Unplugged guitar becomes a teaching resourceThe Royal College of Music announced the donation on 11 December 2025, describing the instrument as one of the most significant artefacts in rock music history. According to the college, the guitar was gifted by Peter Freedman, founder of Australian audio company RØDE Microphones and the Freedman Group.Freedman bought the instrument in 2020 for more than $6 million, establishing a world record for the highest price ever paid for a guitar. Guitar World reported that the final sale price was $6,010,000, making it the most expensive guitar sold at auction.The donation was made in memory of Freedman’s father, Henry Freedman, who died in 1987. The businessman said the gift was intended to honour his father’s love of music and London while supporting the next generation of musicians.The instrument behind Nirvana’s memorable acoustic performanceThe Martin D-18E became closely associated with Cobain after he played it during Nirvana’s MTV Unplugged performance in 1993. The recording, filmed at Sony Music Studios in Manhattan, presented the band in a more stripped-back setting than its familiar electric performances.Guitar World noted that the performance helped immortalise the instrument, turning it into a particularly recognisable piece of music memorabilia. The guitar’s association with Cobain and the performance has continued to attract attention long after the musician’s death.The instrument is also distinctive because it was modified to accommodate Cobain’s left-handed playing. Guitar World reported that the electro-acoustic guitar was adapted for the musician, reflecting the practical changes made to suit his playing style.Its connection to the performance has made it more than an instrument used on stage. It represents a moment in Nirvana’s musical history that continues to resonate with listeners and musicians.A guitar with a remarkable journeyThe instrument's ownership history also forms part of its story. According to Guitar World, Cobain’s daughter, Frances Bean Cobain, inherited the guitar and kept it in a vault in Seattle.In 2018, the guitar was transferred to Isaiah Silva, who claimed ownership as part of a divorce settlement with Frances Bean. The instrument subsequently reached the auction market, where Freedman purchased it two years later.That record-setting sale placed the guitar among the most valuable musical instruments ever sold. Its latest transfer, however, takes it away from private ownership and towards a public and educational role. The donation is an opportunity to share the instrument’s significance with young musicians and audiences internationally.Royal College of Music plans international exhibitionThe donation is also expected to support a wider exhibition programme. The college said plans were being developed for an international touring exhibition featuring Cobain’s guitar from 2026.The proposed tour follows the success of the RCM Museum’s exhibition Kurt Cobain: Unplugged, which attracted more than 15,000 visitors from the UK, Europe and North America.The RCM’s director, James Williams, said the donation created opportunities to share the Kurt Cobain exhibition with an international audience. He also described the gift as reflecting Freedman’s support for performing arts and his belief in education.The guitar joins a collection spanning centuriesCobain’s Martin D-18E will become part of a museum collection that already includes instruments with centuries of history behind them.The Royal College of Music said its museum houses the oldest surviving guitar in existence, a 1581 instrument made in Lisbon by Belchior Dias. The contrast between that historic guitar and Cobain’s modern instrument highlights the breadth of musical history represented at the institution.For students, the collection offers a way to examine how instruments, performance traditions and musical styles have developed over time. Cobain’s guitar adds a relatively recent but influential chapter, connecting the study of music with popular culture and rock history.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Discussed responsibility as world's 3 largest nuclear powers': Trump on first-ever trilateral with Xi, Putin
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday talked about his first-ever trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday talked about his first-ever trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping as a historic step towards global peace, saying the three leaders had agreed to work together to prevent nuclear conflict and reduce the risks posed by nuclear weapons.Addressing a White House press conference after returning from China, Trump highlighted the discussions on nuclear non-proliferation, and the need to ensure that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon. He also expressed optimism about the possibility of ending the Russia-Ukraine war through diplomatic means following his bilateral meeting with Putin."The result of this historic summit was a first of its kind trilateral peace declaration. The United States, Russia, and China formally agreed that nuclear conflict must never be allowed to happen. We don't want it to ever happen. And for the first time ever, China agreed to conduct trilateral discussions on reducing nuclear risks," Trump said.Describing the meeting as one of the most significant international summits in recent years, Trump said there was "great, great electricity" between the three leaders."We discussed the responsibility of the world's three largest nuclear powers by far... to reduce the risk that these weapons pose to the world," he said.However, Trump acknowledged that achieving complete denuclearisation remained difficult, saying he was unsure whether the world could ever get rid of nuclear weapons. He said he viewed them more as a deterrent."I'm the one that keeps talking about the denuclearization of the world, but it's very hard," Trump said. "If somebody comes, I'll make you a deal. Let's all cut them in half. It's hard to say yes, especially when you're leading. So I'm not sure that can ever happen. So I view it more as a deterrent, perhaps."Trump also highlighted China's agreement to hold discussions on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, calling it an achievement even as Beijing seeks to expand its own nuclear arsenal."It's very, very difficult to say, 'Let's get rid of our nuclear weapons. Let's not have any more nuclear weapons,'" he said.Trump also reiterated his position on Iran, saying Washington would not allow Tehran to develop a nuclear weapon."We spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet. And in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They're crazy. We're not going to let them have a nuclear weapon," he said.Also read: 'China will take all of them' - Trump says won't let US firms build data centres abroadTrump on Russia-Ukraine warTrump also expressed hope that the Russia-Ukraine conflict could be resolved through diplomacy, saying Putin had conveyed his desire to end the war during their bilateral meeting."I held a bilateral meeting with President Putin of Russia, who clearly expressed his desire to see the war between Russia and Ukraine end by diplomatic means," Trump said.However, he acknowledged that reaching a settlement would be difficult given the hostility between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. "The problem is President Zelensky and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and that's never easy," he said, adding that the two sides were holding "very good talks"."I think there's a real good chance that we can get it done," Trump added.The US president also claimed that around 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, were being killed every month in the conflict. He blamed his defeat in the 2020 presidential election for the war, saying it would not have happened had he remained in office."Frankly, if the election weren't rigged, where I had to wait four years, that war would never have happened," he said.During the press conferenec, Trump further defended calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether Russian leader is a friend to the US. Asked if Putin was a friend to the American people, Trump, said, "I can't speak to America," but the Russian leader had been "very nice" during what the president called the "Russia hoax" investigation that sprang from Trump's 2016 campaign.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.summary: Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map.

“The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff.

“Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation.

It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine.

“The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.

For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.”

On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span.

During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week.

On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge.

Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.”

Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”.

The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”.

On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway.

In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky.

“Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said.

Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport.

Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active.

Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place.

Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous.

“The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.

This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On October 14, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13.

For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it.

During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel.

Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.

US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have reportedly threatened Ukraine with an intelligence cutoff if it continues to strike Russian refineries.

As Ukraine defied them, Putin and Trump took to the global stage as the guests of Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the city of Shenzhen on November 19.

It was the first time Putin and Trump had met since their summit in Alaska in August 2025, and the first time all three men had met.

Kremlin-aligned media made much of the event, picking up Putin’s comparison with the Big Three conference in Yalta at the end of the second world war.

“The world’s three most consequential powers – have met. As the Big Three, they have emerged as the principal force in shaping a new architecture for international and European security,” wrote Putin’s deputy on the National Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev. “Today … no-one needs Europe.”

Asked whether peace in Ukraine was any closer as a result of the summit, Putin said he and Trump were still aligned on the proposals they discussed in Alaska. Those involved Ukraine handing over to Russia the one-fifth of the eastern Donbas region it cannot take by force, and to agree not to join NATO.

In the recent negotiations at Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, Ukraine was reportedly offered a green light to join NATO in return for the Donbas.

At those talks, Russia also turned its emphasis on Europe’s future security architecture.

Putin developed this further in Shenzhen, reported The New York Times and Bild magazine. He apparently offered Kremlin approval of Ukraine’s EU membership as long as Ukraine did not become part of EU defence policy, and as long as the United Kingdom and France refrained from offering a pan-European nuclear deterrent.

It would be “strange to discuss Europe’s security without Europe itself,” Putin said. On Ukraine’s however, he appeared to demand Europe sign onto whatever the US and Russia agreed.

Despite US and Russian attempts to appear to rearrange the world order, Europe did not appear to be listening.

During the past week , it provided Ukraine with a tranche of 1.7 billion euros ($1.97bn) from a 90 billion euros ($104.4bn) Ukraine Support Loan agreed in 2025, and another 8 billion euros ($9.28bn) from the Ukraine Facility, a 50 billion euros ($58bn) fund focused on Ukrainian economic recovery and financial support.

In addition to these two facilities, the EU agreed this week to raise 45 billion euros ($52.2bn), covering most of a 70-billion-euro ($81.2bn) shortfall that Ukraine says it will face next year. Of that amount, 25 billion euros ($29bn) will be for additional military assistance.

In addition to being a staunch supporter of Ukraine, however, Europe continued to be a divided supporter, deciding that its top diplomat should not represent it in talks with Russia and Ukraine, but representatives from its five biggest economies instead.

Kaja Kallas has argued that “all the member states actually agreed that I am the one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy” when they appointed her to the job of chief of the External Action Service.

“We have institutions in place so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending,” she said this week, in a clear reference to Witkoff and Kushner. “Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

articles.title: Belgrade mayor charged with assaulting opposition politician in Serbia
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Aleksandar Sapic caused serious facial injuries to a female councillor and seek a three-year sentence.
articles.body:
The mayor of Serbia’s capital city, Belgrade, has been charged with injuring a female opposition politician during an argument they had in September.

Serbian prosecutors charged Aleksandar Sapic, a senior figure in the right-wing nationalist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), on Friday. He is accused of grabbing Belgrade city councillor Tatjana Micic by the arm and punching her in the face.

Prosecutors said Micic suffered fractures to her nose and part of her upper jaw, and injuries to her right arm and neck, which the prosecutors said constituted grievous bodily harm.

“Within less than two months of the incident, the Prosecutor’s Office examined witnesses, reviewed video surveillance footage, obtained medical records as well as the findings and opinion of a forensic expert, and filed an indictment proposal,” prosecutors said in a statement.

“In protecting the physical integrity and safety of citizens, the Prosecutor’s Office applies the same criteria to every defendant, regardless of the position they hold,” it added.

They are seeking a three-year sentence for Belgrade mayor Sapic, and are seeking to block him from approaching and communicating with councillor Micic.

Sapic denied attacking Micic, but acknowledged an argument and a scuffle with her husband. Opposition parties have demanded Sapic resign from his role, but he has resisted their calls. Sapic’s SNS party, which had headed up the government since 2012, lost an election to a student-led opposition movement in October.

The party, however, retains control of the capital, Belgrade.
