articles.title: In 2021, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt paid $22.6 million for a Malibu beachfront house; five years later, the 55-foot-oceanfront property is back on the market for $37.5 million amid a second Google-linked listing
articles.summary: Malibu's coveted coastline has long attracted some of the world's wealthiest technology executives, celebrities and business leaders.
articles.body: Malibu's coveted coastline has long attracted some of the world's wealthiest technology executives, celebrities and business leaders. But two high-profile property listings have now put the exclusive California beach community back in the spotlight. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt is seeking $37.5 million for his oceanfront residence, while a second property linked to Google co-founder Sergey Brin has also entered the market. The simultaneous listings have sparked fresh interest in whether some of Silicon Valley's wealthiest figures are reconsidering their California real estate investments amid changing coastal conditions and shifting property priorities.Eric Schmidt seeks $37.5 million for Malibu beachfront estateAccording to the New York Post, Schmidt has listed his residence at 2334 Malibu Colony Drive for $37.5 million. The technology executive purchased the property in 2021 for $22.6 million, significantly below its original asking price of $29 million.The latest listing represents a potential increase of nearly $15 million over his acquisition cost, although the final proceeds will depend on the eventual selling price.Page Six Hollywood also reported that the property is part of a wider wave of luxury listings involving prominent figures from the technology industry.Located inside the guard-gated Malibu Colony community, the 3,495-square-foot residence features five bedrooms, six bathrooms and approximately 55 feet of direct ocean frontage.Inside the property once owned by Gregory PeckThe New York Post reported that the beachfront residence previously belonged to Oscar-winning actor Gregory Peck. Its interiors were designed by Michael S. Smith, who was also selected by former US President Barack Obama to decorate the White House, including the Oval Office.The property features an all-white chef's kitchen, expansive living and dining areas, glass walls overlooking the Pacific Ocean and a large beachfront terrace. Wood panelling, wide-plank flooring and custom millwork contribute to its interiors.A spiral staircase leads to the primary bedroom suite, which includes vaulted ceilings, a sitting area and a spa-inspired bathroom overlooking the ocean. The residence also features a traditional tea house offering views of the surrounding surf.Second Google-linked Malibu property lists for $33.5 millionSchmidt is not the only figure associated with Google whose Malibu real estate holdings have attracted attention.According to Page Six Hollywood and the New York Post, a separate five-bedroom property in Point Dume has been listed for $33.5 million. articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
articles.summary: Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
articles.body:
An Indian national has been sentenced to more ⁠⁠than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder-for-hire plot targeting a prominent Sikh separatist leader living in New York City.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to three conspiracy charges for plotting to hire a hitman to assassinate Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen, lawyer and vocal advocate for a sovereign Sikh state.

US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a federal court in Manhattan on Friday. Gupta faces deportation to India after completing his prison term.

Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader ‌‌Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with an Indian government official to kill Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer for the US-based separatist group Sikhs for Justice, in New York. Pannun is also a proponent of independence for Punjab, the northern Indian state where Sikhism was founded.

Court documents showed that Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in ⁠⁠cash delivered to someone who could kill Pannun. But the person turned out to be an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman.

Gupta was arrested in Prague and has been held without bail since his extradition to the US in June 2023. A plea agreement called for him to serve at least two decades in prison.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer.

India’s government has denied any involvement in the plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

However, multiple alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists have been uncovered in the US and Canada, testing relations with India. New Delhi denies involvement in the plots.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years ⁠⁠in prison for Gupta.

“This case cuts to the very core of ⁠⁠American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”

Pannun was in court on Friday to see the sentence handed down. He described Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.

Pannun said the Modi government wanted him dead “because I lead the campaign openly, defy threats and intimidation”.

Pannun also told the court he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

articles.title: Andy Burnham rejects calls for devolution of powers to Wales in letter to Rhun ap Iorwerth
articles.summary: The prime minister says he is "not persuaded" by the argument that devolution would benefit Wales.
articles.body:
The prime minister has rejected long-standing calls from the first minister of Wales for certain powers to be transferred from Westminster to Cardiff.

In a letter to Rhun ap Iorwerth, Andy Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve responsibilities over policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

The first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution" and not viewing Wales as an "equal nation".

Burnham's position is also at odds with Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates who reiterated his position at a party conference last weekend that policing and the Crown Estate should be devolved.

The letter, seen by BBC Wales, follows what had been seen as positive talks between the prime minister and first minister in Glasgow last month.

Asked about the prime minister's position on devolving policing following that meeting, ap Iorwerth said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there."

Burnham had also previously said he was "open" to the idea.

However, in his letter on Friday, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case.

"The integrated England and Wales policing system is essential to maintaining interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border working and ensuring forces in Wales can draw on national and specialist capabilities," Burnham said.

"Retaining that integrated framework helps ensure policing in Wales can respond effectively to threats and to protecting the public," he added.

On justice, Burnham said he "strongly believes" that the current devolution settlement enables Wales to "benefit from the resources, expertise and resilience" of a shared justice system.

"Effective partnership working is therefore essential to improving outcomes for victims, reducing reoffending and building safer communities."

The Crown Estate includes the seabed off the Welsh coast.

The land belongs to the reigning monarch, and the revenue from its property portfolio goes directly to the UK Treasury.

The previous Welsh Labour government as well as the current Plaid Cymru administration have long called for it to be devolved.

The prime minister told members of his party last week that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.

However, in his letter Burnham said the Crown Estate's "current model provides the best means of maximising the economic and social benefits for Wales".

He went on to say the UK government is "not persuaded by the case for devolving the management of the Crown Estate in Wales, nor to prepare for a future transfer".

Finally, on rail infrastructure, Burnham told the first minister: "I believe funding and delivery of infrastructure is best done by the new Great British Railways, in collaboration with Transport for Wales and Welsh government.

"I am therefore not persuaded by the case for full devolution of rail infrastructure, as it would fragment the current system and affect the service provided to the public by the highly integrated cross border network."

A spokesperson for the first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution".

"His warm words on devolution are now ringing hollow and there is no longer any doubt that when he talks of driving power out of Whitehall, he only means to the regions of England," they said.

The spokesperson added that Burnham's "refusal to even explore the devolution of the Crown Estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation."

articles.title: Tech millionaire spends $14,400 to hire 30 protesters to picket Saks after his mother was fired from the store five days after a customer allegedly punched and kicked her
articles.summary: A tech entrepreneur has launched an unusual protest campaign against luxury retailer Saks Fifth Avenue, spending more than $14,000 to hire demonstrators
articles.body: A tech entrepreneur has launched an unusual protest campaign against luxury retailer Saks Fifth Avenue, spending more than $14,000 to hire demonstrators to picket its stores after his 62-year-old mother was fired just five days after being assaulted by a customer. Jeffrey Vinokur, 36, who sold his educational technology company Generation Genius for $100 million in 2025, has hired more than 30 protesters to demonstrate outside Saks' flagship Manhattan store and its sister retailer Bergdorf Goodman.Vinokur is demanding that Saks CEO Geoffroy van Raemdonck publicly apologize for the treatment of his mother, Laza Susuni, and investigate what he believes is a pattern of employees being dismissed after reporting workplace violence.The entrepreneur initially spent $12,600 to organize demonstrations outside Saks, with protesters carrying placards reading: “My mom is the 7th victim. Beaten at Saks. Then fired. I want answers.” Then he expanded the campaign to Bergdorf Goodman, spending another $1,800 a day on the demonstrations. He expects the number of protesters to reach 90 by November 23. “I want answers,” Vinokur told Daily Voice, adding that he had no intention of stopping the demonstrations until the company addressed his demands.What happened to his mother?The dispute dates back to June 28, when Susuni, who had been working at Saks for just two weeks, got into an altercation with a customer looking for the Casablanca clothing brand. Susuni, a former fashion designer, said she asked the customer about the brand's price range so she could direct her to the appropriate department. The customer reportedly became angry and demanded that management fire her immediately.According to Vinokur, the customer followed his mother towards the dressing-room area, photographed her and demanded to know her last name. Susuni took out her phone and recorded a brief video of the customer because there were no surveillance cameras in that section of the store, her son said.The confrontation then turned violent. The customer allegedly punched Susuni in the face and kicked her in the stomach. Co-workers intervened, and the 62-year-old was taken to hospital.The customer, a 41-year-old woman, was arrested on June 28 and charged with assault and harassment-related offences. On July 15, she pleaded guilty to a violation of New York City's administrative code relating to creating a hazardous or physically offensive condition without a legitimate purpose. She was sentenced to time served, with the remaining charges covered by the plea.Saks fired Susuni five days laterDespite the assault, Saks terminated Susuni's employment five days after the incident, citing serious policy violations and insubordination. The company accused her of recording the customer and refusing to follow her manager's instructions. According to the termination letter, her actions escalated the confrontation and endangered the safety of herself and others.Vinokur and his mother disputed the company's account of her alleged insubordination. They argued that she was documenting an incident in which she was the victim of an assault.Vinokur said his own investigation uncovered six other Saks employees who allegedly experienced workplace violence or sexual harassment before being dismissed. “The trend is that women are victims of sexual abuse or an attack. They report it to HR or to the police, and then they're fired and forced out,” he told Daily Voice. He said five of the cases had been settled, while a sixth was affected by Saks' bankruptcy proceedings.Saks has defended its approach to workplace safety. “We take matters of employee and customer safety and security extremely seriously. It is the company's firmly held policy that we do not retaliate against any employee who reports violations of our policies or the law. articles.title: Wired headphones are making a major comeback — here’s why, plus 5 of the best pairs you can buy
articles.summary: Wired headphones are making a comeback. Here are the top-rated wired earbuds and headphones, including Bose’s new release and Apple’s original earbuds.
articles.body: For most of the last decade, corded headphones have been nearly nonexistent. Phone makers dropped the headphone jack, AirPods became the go-to, and a tangle of wire hanging from your ears started to look dated. Now the cord is making a comeback. After five straight years of falling sales, wired headphone purchases climbed sharply in the second half of 2025, according to the market research firm Circana, and revenue from the category was up about 20% in the first six weeks of 2026. The trend is visible, too: Wired earbuds have been showing up on TikTok and Instagram feeds and Bose released its first wired earbuds in 11 years this fall — and the first batch sold out quickly. If you are interested in kicking it old school with a pair of wired headphones, keep reading, I’ve rounded up top-rated styles worth your consideration. The best wired headphones Every pick on this list connects with a cable. I included a mix of over-ear headphones, on-ear headphones and earbuds. I’ve included options that NBC Selected editors love, as well as highly rated options that have a minimum four-star average rating from one hundred or more shoppers. If the wired comeback has an icon, it’s Apple’s white EarPods. More than 10,000 pairs sold on Amazon in the past month alone. I bought a pair recently after NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown mentioned she had switched back to using them because they’re affordable and less easy to lose. I’ve loved using them to make calls, listen to podcasts and more. When not in use, I love that I can wrap them around my phone. The newest version uses a USB-C plug, so it works with the iPhone 15 and newer, plus most Android phones and laptops, without a dongle. Apple still sells lightning and 3.5mm versions, too. The sound is clear and pleasant and the open design lets in surrounding noise, which some people like for walking or biking around a busy city. Bose launched these in October 2026, its first wired earbuds in 11 years. They connect over USB-C and an in-line remote handles volume, calls and noise-canceling modes. The only other earbuds on this list (besides EarPods), these come with three eartip sizes and two stability bands to help you find a secure fit. They’re also IPX4 sweat-resistant. The ATH-M50x is a go-to studio headphone and it’s just as popular with everyday listeners because it delivers balanced sound. The foam ear cups keep your music in and outside noise out, which makes it practical for an office or a commute. And the detachable cables are a big selling point. Cords are the most common failure point on wired headphones, and with the M50x you can swap in a new one at no extra cost: . It comes with three, including a coiled cable (for desks and studios) and a straight one (for on the go). Koss introduced the Porta Pro in 1984, and it has barely changed since. The chunky foam earpads and metal headband look like they came straight from a Walkman ad, which has made them a favorite among people leaning into the retro side of the wired revival. Reviewers like bass-forward sound and value, and Koss backs them with a lifetime warranty. Just know that because the earcups are open, the people next to you will hear some of what you’re listening to. If you’re a sound snob, these headphones from Sennheiser are worth considering. Reviewers call the crisp, clear sound of these “incredible,” and say they have “impressive clarity.” The over-ear design creates a spacious, natural sound, almost like listening to speakers in the room. They are also lightweight and velour ear pads keep you comfortable for hours-long wear. How I picked the best wired headphones Our editors have tested a lot of headphones over the years and reported on some of the top audio brands. To come up with a list of the best wired headphones, I focused on brands we’ve covered before and kept the following things in mind: Price and value: One of the biggest reasons people are switching back to wired is cost, so I prioritized picks that give you the most for your money at each price point.Connectivity: I noted whether each pair uses a 3.5mm or USB-C plug, since different devices will require different connection types.Reputation: Many of these models have been on the market for years or even decades, with long track records from professionals and everyday listeners.Variety: I included earbuds, on-ear and over-ear headphones for different budgets and uses, from commuting to gaming to studio work. The benefits of wired headphones Not fully sold on wired headphones? Here are more of the benefits they offer: They’re harder to lose. A single wireless earbud can slip out of a pocket, roll under a subway seat or vanish into a couch. A wired pair stays together, and the cord keeps it tethered to your phone.They tend to cost less. You can find a pair of wired headphones for as little as $10 on Amazon — with a number of bestselling brands offering options for around $20. Even high-end wired headphones tend to cost less than wireless versions with similar sound.They never need charging. There’s no battery dying halfway through a flight and no case to remember to plug in at night.They just work. There’s also no pairing, no dropped Bluetooth connections in crowded places and no audio lag when you’re gaming or watching video. Want more from NBC Selected? LANE KIFFIN BLAMES LSU'S $40+ MILLION ROSTER AFTER LOSS TO TEXAS: 'WE'LL HAVE BETTER ROSTERS’ Even potential wins against top-ten Tennessee this weekend and Golden Boot rivals Arkansas after Thanksgiving would do little to improve LSU's standing in the CFP polls. So, what went wrong? They hired the best available coach, paired him with an all-star staff that included one of the best defensive coordinators in the game in Blake Baker and armed him with one of the most expensive rosters in college football. Shouldn't that be enough to expect a home run in year one? College football commentator Josh Pate isn't buying the idea that an expensive roster guarantees success in this day and age. JOSH PATE WAS EVICTED WHILE EARNING $27K. NOW, HE RUNS A COLLEGE FOOTBALL MEDIA EMPIRE "I guess he enters next year on the hot seat," Pate said sarcastically while replying to a question from one of his viewers. "I'm not asking anyone to feel sorry for Lane Kiffin," he continued. Pate would go on to explain that giving someone unlimited resources doesn't always equate to leveling up, and Kiffin is no different. "People kept throwing around that same data point: $40 million roster... What it was (was) LSU going and hiring their dream candidate at head coach, and then them just recklessly throwing around as much money as they could in the portal to put together a team to compete for a national title in year one." It sounds like a simple formula, even to those who have been paying attention to the sport for a few years now in the NIL era, but it might not be that cut and dry. "If this same exact roster was paid $28 million, would it be different? No, it's the same roster," he points out. Plain and simple, the Tigers might have overpaid for some of the talent on their two-deep. "You just paid a lot of money for 'average.'" As Pate explains, LSU's pickups in the portal were great, but they only papered over deficiencies rather than provided quality depth, and, more importantly, they missed at the most important position: quarterback. ARCH MANNING TURNS DEATH VALLEY INTO LSU’S FUNERAL AS TEXAS BURIES LANE KIFFIN’S CFP HOPES "They didn't whiff on this portal class, by the way," he argues. "A lot of these dudes have been studs. It's just the most important position, there's not a stud at." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP To his credit, Pate has been consistent with his takes on Kiffin and LSU. The popular YouTube host said back in July that he thought the Tigers would miss the playoff outright in year one, and that caused some consternation among the LSU faithful. Where LSU goes from here remains a mystery, but you can rest assured that Pate's words will fall on deaf ears. Kiffin is making too much money and has been given too many resources to fail this badly in year one. He will be going into a pivotal year two with the expectations ratcheted up considerably. Should he miss the CFP again in 2027, it might be time for Kiffin to start looking for a good realtor in southern Louisiana.

articles.body: One random afternoon, you are just minding your business, harvesting some crops, cleaning the field, collecting grains, and casually, a rare guest decides to pay you a visit. We all love when that happens, right? But jokes aside, that's exactly what happened to a Kansas family.The family was making the final few passes through their field when they spotted an animal jumping through the crops. Initially, they were unsure what they were looking at and began discussing it over the radio. It was only when the animal emerged from the milo crop that they realised it was a bear.Brooklin Moritz, one of the family members who witnessed the encounter, described the moment to KWCH 12 News, saying, “We were all arguing about it over the radio on what it was, and then it jumped out of the milo and it was like, ‘oh, it's a bear.’”The footage of the encounter eventually drew the attention of wildlife experts. What made the bear particularly remarkable was its unusual coat, which displayed distinct patches of light and dark fur. Matt Peek, a wildlife research biologist with the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks, who helped identify the bear, said it was the first piebald bear he had ever seen in Kansas.What is a piebald black bear, and what was it doing in Kansas?According to the NIH, US, piebaldism is a rare genetic condition that causes an animal to have patches of differently coloured fur, creating an unusual pattern across its body. Unlike an ordinary black bear, whose coat is generally dark, a piebald bear can have contrasting light and dark patches. The condition is associated with differences in pigmentation, making the animal's appearance particularly distinctive.But the unusual coat was only one part of the story. The presence of a black bear in western Kansas was itself an uncommon sight. According to Matt Peek, a wildlife research biologist, bears spotted in that part of the state have previously been known to have cinnamon-coloured fur. However, the latest sighting stood out because of the animal's piebald colouring.So, what was the bear doing there in the first place? Peek explained that many of the bears spotted in the region are young, yearling animals that have left their mothers and their original home ranges. They are essentially dispersing in search of territories of their own, while also looking for food.“Most of what we see is these yearling, dispersal-aged bears that have left their, you know, they've left their mother and their natal home range,” Peek told KWCH 12 News. “And they're out searching for their own home range, or this time of year and a little earlier, they're moving around looking for food.”This means the bear's appearance in the family's agricultural field may have been part of its movement in search of food or a new home range, rather than evidence of an established bear population in the area. Peek also confirmed that this was the first piebald bear he had ever seen in Kansas.A rare sighting that caught wildlife experts by surpriseSuch sightings for wildlife biologists are like finding a $10 bill lying on the roadside. They are unexpected, rare and certainly worth stopping for. While black bears themselves are not entirely unknown in Kansas, spotting one with such unusual colouring is a different matter altogether.For wildlife experts, the unusual colouring was what made this encounter particularly noteworthy. According to Matt Peek, bears spotted in this part of Kansas have a history of having cinnamon-coloured fur. However, the animal captured in the family's video had a distinctly different appearance, with contrasting patches of light and dark fur. Its identification as a piebald black bear made it an especially unusual sighting, even by the standards of an already rare bear encounter in the state.Human curiosity has no end; we can pet whatever feels cute, but Peek highlighted the importance of keeping a safe distance from bears when they appear near farms or residential areas. He advised people to secure food supplies, take precautions to prevent bears from accessing animal feed and silage, and never feed them. These measures can help prevent unwanted interactions between humans and wildlife and promote mutual safety.For the Kansas family, however, what began as an ordinary day in the fields turned into an encounter they are unlikely to forget anytime soon. The news soon became the talk of the town, making the family's day even busier than usual. articles.title: Texas inmate complained of pain during execution: witnesses
articles.summary: A convicted murderer complained of excruciating pain as he was put to death by lethal injection in Texas in an execution that took more than an hour, witness...
articles.body:
A convicted murderer complained of excruciating pain as he was put to death by lethal injection in Texas in an execution that took more than an hour, witnesses said.

Reinaldo Dennes, 70, was executed at a state prison in Huntsville on Thursday evening for the 1996 murder of a diamond dealer during a robbery that netted more than $3.6 million.

Dennes was killed by the same drug -- pentobarbital -- that was used in the failed execution in Tennessee of another condemned murderer, Christa Pike, in September.

Pike survived the attempted execution. She was hospitalized in critical condition but has since been returned to prison.

Prison officials deny allegations of mishandling, but Reverend Jeff Hood, Dennes's spiritual adviser, who was in the execution chamber as he was being put to death, described the execution as "botched" in a Zoom call with reporters on Friday.

"This thing went off the rails very quickly," said Hood, who has attended more than a dozen other executions. "Immediately, Ronaldo began to scream, 'My leg, my leg, my leg is on fire.'"

Hood said Dennes was "clearly in tremendous distress."

"Twice he said, 'It's not working, it's not working, it's not going how it's supposed to go," Hood said.

Dennes continued speaking for four or five minutes after the lethal drugs began to flow and then began to groan, he said.

"In a typical lethal injection done correctly you see someone lose consciousness very quickly," Hood said. "But never do you see this amount of time, except if it's a botched execution."

Michael Graczyk, a reporter with the US news agency The Associated Press who attended the execution, also said it was unusual.

Graczyk said he has witnessed nearly 500 executions by lethal injection and Dennes's was "dramatically different."

Dennes complained of "excruciating pain" as he was injected with the lethal drugs, he said.

Amanda Hernandez, spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ), said the execution took a little over an hour in total because there was initially some difficulty finding suitable veins for the IV needles that delivered the pentobarbital.

"TDCJ denies any claim of the execution being 'botched,'" Hernandez said. "The agency followed all of its protocols and the execution was successfully carried out.

"IVs were inserted into the most viable veins available, in the left foot and left side of the neck," she said. "Dennes made allegations of pain in locations where there were no IVs established and prior to any drugs being administered."

She said the lethal dosage began to flow at 6:52 pm Central Time and Dennes was pronounced dead 16 minutes later.

There have been 39 executions in the United States this year, all by lethal injection.

Support for the death penalty among Americans has fallen to its lowest level in 55 years, according to a recent poll.

Forty-nine percent of US adults are in favor of the death penalty for convicted murderers and 45 percent are opposed, the Gallup poll found.
